hints: Look closely at line X-Y in the drawing and measure its length on the page in millimetres with a ruler. This is your magnified image size.
Remember that image size = real size x magnification, so you will need to divide your measurement by x1500 and then see how many of those real cell widths fit into 1 cm.
walkthrough:
**Measure the image and recall the magnification rule**

Great start, let's get our numbers. Measure line X-Y on the paper. It is about $30 \text{ mm}$.

Remember the golden rule:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{real size}}$$

**Calculate the real width of one cell**

Now we work backwards to find the true size. Rearrange the formula:
$$\text{real size} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}}$$

Put in your values:
$$\text{real size} = \frac{30 \text{ mm}}{1500} = 0.02 \text{ mm}$$

Convert to micrometres to make sense of it, $0.02 \text{ mm} = 20 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$, a very sensible width for an epithelial cell.

**Find how many fit in 1 cm**

Finally, how many $0.02 \text{ mm}$ cells fit along $1 \text{ cm}$? First convert to the same units, $1 \text{ cm} = 10 \text{ mm}$.

Then divide:
$$\text{number of cells} = \frac{10 \text{ mm}}{0.02 \text{ mm}} = 500$$

options.A: Too small. 5 cells in 1 cm would mean each cell is 2 mm wide, far too large for an epithelial cell seen with an electron microscope.
options.B: Too small. 50 cells would give a real width of 0.2 mm (200 micrometres), which is about 10 times too wide. You may have missed a zero in conversion.
options.C: Correct. A 30 mm image at x1500 gives a real width of 0.02 mm, and 10 mm divided by 0.02 mm gives 500 cells per cm.
options.D: Too large. 5000 cells would mean each cell is only 2 micrometres wide, far too narrow for this ciliated cell. You may have multiplied instead of dividing correctly.
